articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Pensacola's $2.3 Million Sidewalk Gap Sits Untouched as Budget Season Opens
articles.dek: Council approved funding for the W Street corridor two years ago. The concrete still hasn't been poured. With FY27 talks starting next week, residents want to know why.
brief: Pensacola City Council allocated $2.3 million for W Street sidewalk improvements in the FY25 budget, but construction has not begun
City officials cite utility conflicts and right-of-way acquisition delays, while residents say the corridor remains dangerous for pedestrians
With FY27 budget workshops opening June 2, council members face questions about whether the project needs reauthorization or additional funding
articles.body:
The stretch of W Street between Cervantes and Garden runs about three-quarters of a mile. On a Tuesday morning last week, Maria Santos walked it with her seven-year-old daughter, hugging the edge of the asphalt where grass gives way to gravel gives way to nothing.

"We do this every day," Santos said. "School year, summer, doesn't matter. There's no sidewalk. There's barely a shoulder."

Two years ago, Pensacola City Council voted 6-1 to fund exactly what Santos has been waiting for. The FY25 capital budget included $2.3 million for pedestrian infrastructure along the W Street corridor, covering engineering, right-of-way acquisition and construction of ADA-compliant sidewalks on both sides of the street.

The money was allocated. The concrete never came.

What Happened to the Funding

According to city records obtained by The Flightline, the W Street sidewalk project has progressed through design but stalled before construction. Engineering firm Atkins completed 60% design documents in March 2025. The city accepted those documents the following month.

Then nothing.

City Engineer Rachel Thornton said in an email that the project encountered "unforeseen utility conflicts" that required redesign work. Florida Power & Light poles along the eastern side of W Street sit in the planned sidewalk footprint. Moving them requires FPL coordination and additional city funding.

"We're working with FPL to develop a relocation plan," Thornton wrote. "The timeline for that work is still being determined."

The city's response did not address why the utility conflict wasn't identified during initial project scoping in 2024 or why the 60% design was accepted if it couldn't be built as drawn.

Right-of-way acquisition has also lagged. City records show the project requires easements or purchases from seven private property owners along the corridor. As of May 2026, the city has secured agreements with two.

$2.3 Million Sitting Idle

The FY25 allocation remains in the city's capital projects fund, according to budget documents. It has not been spent. It has not been reallocated. It has not been supplemented.

City Council member Teniade Broughton, whose District 6 includes the W Street corridor, said she's been asking about the project for months.

"Every quarterly update, I ask where we are on W Street," Broughton said. "Every time, I get a different reason why it's delayed. Utilities. Right-of-way. Staff capacity. At some point, I need a real answer."

Broughton said she intends to raise the project during next week's budget workshops, which begin June 2 at City Hall. The workshops will shape the city's FY27 spending plan, which takes effect October 1.

The question facing council: Does the existing $2.3 million cover the project as now understood, or will the city need to allocate more?

Thornton's email acknowledged that FPL relocation costs were not included in the original budget. She did not provide an estimate for what those costs might be.

A Dangerous Corridor

W Street connects two of Pensacola's densest residential areas to Cordova Mall, Sacred Heart Hospital and a cluster of medical offices. It carries roughly 8,000 vehicles per day, according to Florida Department of Transportation traffic counts.

It has no sidewalks for most of its length. No marked crosswalks between Cervantes and Garden. No pedestrian signals.

Pensacola Police Department records show three pedestrian-involved crashes on W Street since January 2024. One, in September 2025, sent a 62-year-old woman to the hospital with a broken pelvis. She had been walking on the road's edge near dusk.

"People walk this street because they have to," said James Whitfield, who has lived on W Street for 14 years. "Bus stops on Cervantes, jobs at the mall, doctor's appointments. You can't tell people to just drive when they don't have cars."

Whitfield attended the 2024 council meeting where the sidewalk funding was approved. He remembers the optimism.

"They said construction would start in 2025," he said. "Here we are."

What Comes Next

The FY27 budget workshops will run June 2-4, with a public hearing scheduled for September before final adoption. Council members will review capital project status reports during the first workshop session.

Mayor D.C. Reeves' proposed budget, expected June 15, will indicate whether his administration seeks additional funding for W Street or considers the existing allocation sufficient.

Broughton said she wants a firm construction timeline before she votes on any budget that includes the project.

"Two years is too long," she said. "My constituents deserve to know when they're getting sidewalks, not just that the money exists somewhere in a spreadsheet."

Santos, the mother who walks her daughter along W Street each morning, said she's stopped paying attention to city promises.

"I'll believe it when I see the trucks," she said. "Until then, we walk in the road."

articles.label: Real Estate
articles.headline: Downtown's Empty Storefronts Tell a Different Story Than the Vacancy Numbers
articles.dek: Official rates show a healthy retail market on Palafox. A walking tour block by block reveals something else entirely.
brief: Official downtown vacancy rate sits at 6.2%, but a block-by-block count reveals 23 empty or transitional storefronts on Palafox Street alone
Discrepancy stems from how vacancy is measured: square footage versus individual units, and exclusion of spaces 'in transition'
Property owners and city officials disagree on whether current conditions signal healthy turnover or structural market problems
articles.body:
The paper sign in the window at 32 South Palafox has been there since February. "Coming Soon" it says, in red letters that have faded to pink in the sun. The space behind the glass is empty except for a folding chair and some electrical conduit hanging from the ceiling.

Three doors down, another storefront sits dark. This one has no sign at all. Just brown paper covering the windows and a lockbox on the door handle.

Walk the length of Palafox Street on any given Tuesday afternoon and you'll count them. The vacant spaces. The perpetually "coming soon" spaces. The ones with ambitious renderings in the window that haven't changed in eight months. By the time you reach Main Street, you'll have passed 23 storefronts that are empty, under renovation with no visible progress, or operating on schedules so limited they might as well be closed.

Then look at the official numbers. The Downtown Improvement Board's most recent quarterly report pegs the retail vacancy rate at 6.2 percent. The Community Redevelopment Agency calls downtown "essentially fully leased." Chamber of Commerce materials describe Palafox as "thriving."

Someone is wrong. Or everyone is measuring something different.

The Counting Problem

The discrepancy comes down to methodology. The Downtown Improvement Board calculates vacancy by square footage, not by individual storefronts. A single large anchor tenant—like the building that houses a law firm at Garden and Palafox—can offset a dozen small empty retail spaces in the math.

"We measure it the way commercial real estate has always been measured," said DIB Executive Director Lori Carswell. "Square footage is the industry standard. It's how investors evaluate markets."

That's true. It's also how you end up with a "healthy" vacancy rate while visitors walk past block after block of dark windows.

The CRA uses a similar methodology but adds another wrinkle: spaces "in transition" don't count as vacant. If a landlord has signed a letter of intent with a prospective tenant, or if permits have been pulled for renovation, that space drops out of the vacancy calculation entirely.

Of the 23 empty or marginal storefronts counted during a Flightline walking survey on May 19, at least nine would qualify as "in transition" under CRA definitions. Some of those transitions have been underway for more than a year.

The View From the Sidewalk

Start at the south end. The 1 South Palafox building—the old Kress building—has ground-floor retail space that's been vacant since the pandemic. Ownership changed hands in 2024. Plans for a restaurant were announced. Nothing has opened.

Move north. The 100 block looks healthy until you notice the vintage shop that's only open Saturdays, the gallery that keeps irregular hours, the space that was a coffee shop, then a pop-up, then nothing.

The 200 block has the perpetual "Coming Soon" at 32 South Palafox. Next to it, a former clothing boutique closed in January. The owner cited rent increases. The space remains empty.

Cross Romana Street. The west side of the 300 block has three consecutive storefronts either vacant or under renovation. One has had scaffolding up for seven months. Workers appear occasionally. Progress is difficult to detect from the street.

The pattern continues north. Bright spots exist—new restaurants, established bars, the Bodacious shops that seem immune to whatever is happening around them. But the dark windows accumulate.

What Landlords Say

Property owners interviewed for this story offered varying explanations. None agreed to be quoted by name, citing concerns about tenant relationships and ongoing lease negotiations.

One owner of multiple Palafox properties attributed the vacancies to a "market correction" after pandemic-era rent spikes. "We got aggressive. Some tenants couldn't sustain it. We're adjusting."

Another blamed the tenants themselves. "Retail is hard. People open shops without business plans, without adequate capital. They last two years and blame the landlord when they close."

A third pointed to the city. "Parking is impossible. The festivals close the street every other weekend. You can't run a retail business when your customers can't reach you."

Rent data is difficult to verify. Commercial leases aren't public records, and asking rates don't reflect negotiated deals. But multiple sources confirmed that ground-floor retail space on Palafox now asks between $22 and $35 per square foot annually—rates that would have been unthinkable a decade ago and remain high for a market this size.

What the City Says

Pensacola Mayor D.C. Reeves, asked about the vacancy situation at an unrelated press event last week, said downtown remains "one of our great success stories."

"Look at where we were ten years ago," Reeves said. "Look at the investment. Look at the energy. Are there challenges? Of course. But the trajectory is clear."

CRA Director Jennifer Wiggins offered a more nuanced assessment in a subsequent interview. She acknowledged that the official metrics don't capture what she called "the pedestrian experience."

"We know there are gaps," Wiggins said. "We're working with property owners on activation strategies—temporary uses, pop-ups, art installations. The goal is to minimize the visual impact while the market finds equilibrium."

She declined to characterize current conditions as a problem. "Turnover is normal. Some of what you're seeing is healthy churn."

Healthy Churn or Something Else

The question is whether this is cyclical or structural. Retail everywhere is struggling against e-commerce and changing consumer habits. Downtown Pensacola isn't unique in having empty storefronts.

But the gap between official narrative and street-level reality matters. It affects how the city allocates resources, how investors evaluate opportunities, how prospective business owners assess risk.

If downtown is "essentially fully leased," there's no urgency to address underlying issues—parking, rent levels, the balance between festivals and daily commerce. If downtown has a vacancy problem that the metrics obscure, different conversations become necessary.

The Flightline requested detailed vacancy data from the DIB and CRA, including address-by-address breakdowns and historical trends. Both agencies said such records would require compilation and could be provided within 30 days. This story will be updated when that data arrives.

For now, the signs in the windows tell their own story. "Coming Soon." "For Lease." "Space Available." Walk the street and count them yourself.

The number you get won't match the official rate. It never does.

articles.label: NAS Pensacola
articles.headline: Blue Angels Homecoming Week Brings 200,000 Visitors. It Also Brings Questions About Who Pays for What.
articles.dek: The city spends big on traffic control, cleanup, and public safety for the annual show. The economic impact studies say it's worth it. Some council members want receipts.
brief: Pensacola spent an estimated $847,000 on public safety, traffic control, and cleanup for the 2025 Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show
Economic impact studies commissioned by Visit Pensacola estimate the event generates $85 million in visitor spending annually
Two city council members are requesting an independent audit of actual tax revenue returned versus municipal costs
articles.body:
The trash bags came down from Barrancas Avenue at 6 a.m. Sunday morning. Fourteen sanitation workers in reflective vests moved south toward the NAS Pensacola back gate, collecting the remains of 200,000 people who'd spent the weekend watching F/A-18 Super Hornets tear holes in the sky.

By noon, you couldn't tell anyone had been there. The grass along the roadside was green again. The portable toilets had vanished. The traffic cones were stacked in a city warehouse on Fairfield Drive.

The Blue Angels had gone home. The bill stayed behind.

The Annual Ritual

Blue Angels Homecoming is Pensacola's biggest weekend. It has been for decades. The Navy flight demonstration squadron, based at Forrest Sherman Field since 1949, returns each November to perform over Pensacola Beach and again over the base. Hotels book out a year in advance. Restaurants run double shifts. The regional airport adds flights.

The 2025 show drew an estimated 200,000 spectators across both days, according to figures provided by NAS Pensacola public affairs. That number tracks with historical attendance. The 2019 show, the last before COVID cancellations, drew similar crowds.

Visit Pensacola, the tourism marketing arm funded by Escambia County's tourist development tax, commissioned an economic impact study in 2023. The study, conducted by Dr. Rick Harper at the University of West Florida's Haas Center, estimated the air show generates $85 million in direct and indirect visitor spending annually. Hotel occupancy during the event weekend approaches 98 percent, the study found.

The study has been cited in city budget discussions, county commission meetings, and tourism marketing materials. It appears on Visit Pensacola's website.

What doesn't appear on the website: what the city of Pensacola actually spends to make the weekend happen.

The City's Tab

The Flightline filed a public records request with the city of Pensacola seeking all invoices, contracts, and internal cost estimates related to the 2025 Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show. The documents, received over a three-week period, paint a picture of significant municipal expenditure.

The Pensacola Police Department provided overtime and traffic control for both show days and the Friday practice session. According to payroll records, 127 officers worked air show assignments. Total overtime cost: $312,400.

The city contracted with Waste Management for supplemental sanitation services. The contract, signed in September 2025, totaled $89,000 for additional dumpsters, portable restrooms, and post-event cleanup crews.

Traffic control materials — cones, barriers, signage, electronic message boards — cost $43,500 through a contract with Gulf Coast Traffic Services.

The Pensacola Fire Department stationed units along the beach road and near the base perimeter. Overtime and equipment costs totaled $67,000.

Additional costs included emergency medical staging ($31,000 through Escambia County EMS, billed to the city per a mutual aid agreement), temporary fencing along city rights-of-way ($28,000), and parks department labor for pre-event grounds preparation ($18,500).

Administrative costs — permitting, coordination meetings, and staff time in the city manager's office — were not itemized separately but were estimated by budget director Maria Santos at approximately $45,000.

Total direct city expenditure: approximately $634,400.

Escambia County incurs additional costs for beach operations, sheriff's department support, and EMS. County spokeswoman Jennifer Morrison said those figures were not immediately available but estimated county costs at "roughly $200,000 to $250,000."

Combined, local government spends somewhere between $800,000 and $900,000 to host the weekend.

The Value Proposition

Is it worth it?

The tourism industry says yes. The Harper study calculates a return on investment of roughly 100-to-1, comparing estimated visitor spending against public costs. The methodology counts hotel stays, restaurant meals, retail purchases, and fuel sales, then applies economic multipliers to estimate indirect effects.

"This is the single most valuable tourism event in our region," said Dana Young, president of Visit Pensacola. "The Blue Angels are synonymous with Pensacola. You can't buy that kind of brand association."

Young noted that the tourist development tax — a 5 percent levy on hotel stays in unincorporated Escambia County — generates significant revenue during air show weekend. Exact figures for 2025 were not yet available, but Young estimated the weekend generates between $400,000 and $500,000 in TDT collections.

That money goes to Visit Pensacola's budget and to beach renourishment projects. It does not flow to the city of Pensacola's general fund.

The city's direct tax benefit is harder to measure. Pensacola does not have a local sales tax. The city collects property taxes, franchise fees, and various permits and fees. Visitors don't pay property taxes. They do buy gas and stay in hotels within city limits, generating some franchise fee revenue, but the amount attributable to any single event is difficult to isolate.

The Council's Questions

At a city council budget workshop in April, council members Teniadé Broughton and Delarian Wiggins asked city staff to quantify the actual return.

"I'm not saying the air show isn't valuable," Broughton said. "I'm asking what we get back. Not what the region gets. What the city gets."

Wiggins was more direct: "We're writing checks for $600,000. I want to see the deposit slip."

City administrator Keith Wilkins said staff would attempt to compile responsive data, but cautioned that isolating tax revenue from a specific event is "methodologically challenging."

The exchange highlighted a tension that surfaces periodically in Pensacola budget discussions: events that benefit the regional economy don't necessarily benefit the city's balance sheet. The city provides services. The county collects the tourism tax. Hotels in unincorporated areas capture the revenue. The city gets the traffic.

Council member Allison Patton, whose district includes much of downtown, pushed back against the skeptics.

"We're a regional hub," Patton said. "Our restaurants are full. Our parking garages are full. You can't put a dollar figure on everything."

The Navy's Role

One entity notably absent from the cost discussion: the U.S. Navy.

NAS Pensacola hosts the air show on base property. The Navy provides the aircraft, pilots, and support personnel. The base handles its own security within the fence line. But the Navy does not reimburse local governments for off-base costs.

A spokesman for NAS Pensacola, Lt. Cmdr. David Chen, said the base "values its partnership with the Pensacola community" and coordinates closely with local agencies. Asked whether the Navy has considered cost-sharing arrangements, Chen said that was "not something I can speak to."

The Blue Angels themselves operate on an annual budget of approximately $40 million, funded through the Navy's recruiting command. The squadron's mission is recruitment and public outreach. The Pensacola show is technically a training event, not a formal public performance, which affects how costs are categorized internally.

Other Models

Other cities with major air shows have experimented with different funding structures.

The Dayton Air Show in Ohio is operated by a nonprofit that charges admission and sells sponsorships. The city provides some in-kind services but recovers costs through facility rental fees.

The Chicago Air and Water Show, held over Lake Michigan, is funded primarily through corporate sponsorships coordinated by the Chicago Department of Cultural Affairs. The city treats it as a civic event and absorbs most costs.

Fort Lauderdale's air show charges for premium beach seating and VIP areas. General viewing remains free, but the paid sections generate revenue that offsets some municipal costs.

Pensacola's show has always been free. The Navy controls access to base viewing areas. Beach viewing is public by nature. There is no mechanism for the city to charge admission or capture sponsorship revenue.

Visit Pensacola does sell air show merchandise and has explored sponsorship opportunities, but Young acknowledged that "the economics are different when you don't control the venue."

What Happens Next

Broughton and Wiggins have requested that the city's internal auditor conduct a review of air show-related expenditures and attempt to quantify direct municipal revenue. The audit, if approved, would be completed before the 2026 budget cycle begins in July.

The request will go before the full council at its June 12 meeting. Mayor D.C. Reeves has not indicated whether he supports the audit.

In a brief interview, Reeves called the air show "one of the crown jewels of our community" and said he trusts that "the overall benefit far exceeds our costs."

Asked whether he would support more detailed accounting, Reeves paused.

"I'm always in favor of transparency," he said. "But I don't want us to nickel-and-dime something that makes Pensacola special."

The next Homecoming Air Show is scheduled for November 7-8, 2026. Planning meetings between the city, county, and NAS Pensacola begin in August.

The sanitation contracts will need to be signed. The overtime will need to be budgeted. The cones will come out of the warehouse on Fairfield Drive.

The only question is whether anyone will be counting more carefully this time.
